content: Addressin, also referred to as mucosal vascular addressin cell adhesion molecule 1 (MAdCAM-1), is a protein encoded by the MADCAM1 gene in humans. This protein is an extracellular molecule found on the endothelium of venules. Addressins serve as ligands for the homing receptors present on lymphocytes. The primary function of these ligands and their corresponding receptors is to determine the specific tissue that a lymphocyte will migrate to next. Addressins carry carbohydrate structures that allow them to be recognized by L-selectin. The protein encoded by the MADCAM1 gene is an endothelial cell adhesion molecule that preferentially interacts with leukocyte beta-7 integrin LPAM-1 (alpha4/beta7), L-selectin, and VLA-4 (alpha4/beta1) on myeloid cells. These interactions facilitate the directed migration of leukocytes into mucosal and inflamed tissues. MAdCAM-1 belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily and shares structural similarities with ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. In terms of cellular migration, MAdCAM-1 is selectively expressed on mucosal endothelial cells, where it plays a critical role in driving the recirculation of memory T-cells through mucosal tissues. In contrast, ICAM molecules are primarily involved in the recirculation of naive T-cells. A key distinction between these two molecules is their expression patterns: MAdCAM-1 is selectively expressed in mucosal tissues, whereas ICAM molecules are broadly expressed on inflamed endothelium.
